edges.description: The model reproduces postnatal multisuture synostosis but requires a lower residual Erf dosage (~30%) than the human disease (~50% from heterozygous loss of function).
edges.limitations: The dosage threshold differs from humans: heterozygous Erf+/- mice (about 50% dosage, equivalent to the human genotype) are phenotypically normal, so quantitative inferences about the human derepression threshold do not transfer directly.

edges.description: At the dosage that causes human disease (heterozygous loss of function, ~50%), the mouse develops no synostosis, so Erf+/- does not model the human fusion phenotype.

nodes.description: A heterozygous loss-of-function ERF variant (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, translation-initiation, ETS-domain missense, or whole-gene deletion) reduces functional ERF2 repressor dosage to roughly half. ERF is normally held inactive in the cytoplasm by ERK1/2-mediated phosphorylation and nuclear export downstream of RAS-MEK-ERK signaling; its repressor activity depends on nuclear accumulation of unphosphorylated protein. Reduced dosage therefore lowers the amount of repressor available to the nucleus.

nodes.description: Nuclear ERF normally represses osteogenic transcriptional programs in suture mesenchyme, competing with activating ETS factors (such as ETS2) and modulating RUNX2-associated regulatory complexes at distal enhancers enriched for RUNX and AP-1 motifs. In the wild type, Erf is expressed along the osteogenic margins of the developing calvarial bones in a distribution resembling that of the master osteogenic regulator Runx2. Reduced ERF dosage relaxes this anti-osteogenic restraint - the restraint-loss entry point into the shared cranial-suture premature-fusion endpoint, distinct from the pro-osteogenic-signalling drive of the FGFR and BMP routes.
